'''Loren James Toews''' (born November 3, 1951) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[linebacker]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[California Golden Bears football|California Golden Bears]].

Toews graduated from [[Del Mar High School]] in [[San Jose, California]]<ref>{{Cite web |last=Sparrer |first=Dick |date=September 2, 2013 |orig-date=September 2, 2013 |title=Cattolico leaves a legacy on the football field, and on report cards |url=https://www.mercurynews.com/2013/09/02/cattolico-leaves-a-legacy-on-the-football-field-and-on-report-cards/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170504133349/https://www.mercurynews.com/2013/09/02/cattolico-leaves-a-legacy-on-the-football-field-and-on-report-cards/ |archive-date=May 4, 2017 |access-date=2024-10-06 |website=The Mercury News |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Tennis |first=Mark |title=Yanks, Celtics, Pats On One State List |url=https://www.calhisports.com/2015/10/15/yanks-celtics-pats-on-one-state-list/ |access-date=2024-10-06 |website=Cal-Hi Sports |language=en-US}}</ref> and later the [[University of California, Berkeley]], where he received his degree in biological sciences.  In 1972, Toews was named the "most inspirational player" for the [[California Golden Bears football|Golden Bears]] and given the Stub Allison Award,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.calbears.com/sports/m-footbl/archive/052908aaa.html |title=Cal Football Team Awards |access-date=December 2, 2010 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120223065244/http://www.calbears.com/sports/m-footbl/archive/052908aaa.html |archive-date=February 23, 2012 }}</ref> named after California football coach [[Stub Allison|Leonard B. "Stub" Allison]].

That following year, in 1973 Toews was selected in the eighth round by the [[Pittsburgh Steelers]] where he played as a [[linebacker]] for 11 seasons.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1984/05/29/sports/sports-people-toews-retires.html |title=Toews Retires |date=May 29, 1984 |work=[[The New York Times]] |access-date=December 2, 2010}}</ref>  While playing for the Steelers, Toews attended the [[University of Pittsburgh]]'s Graduate School of Business and obtained his [[Master of Business Administration|MBA]] degree in 1981.

Toews was a four-time [[Super Bowl]] champion,<ref name="upiretire"/> and starter in [[Super Bowl XIII]]. In [[Super Bowl IX]] he replaced an injured [[Andy Russell (American football)|Andy Russell]] for most of the second half, filling in admirably.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://steelersdepot.com/2014/04/steelers-greatest-draft-hits-eighth-round/ |title=Steelers Greatest Draft Hits – Eighth Round |last=Reynolds |first=Michael K. |date=April 5, 2014 |website=steelersdepot.com |access-date=November 1, 2017}}</ref> Toews moved to left inside linebacker in 1982 when the Steelers switched to the [[3–4 defense]], while incumbent middle linebacker [[Jack Lambert (American football)|Jack Lambert]] moved to right inside linebacker and retained the "Mike" role as the Steelers signal-caller on defense.

Toews retired from professional football at spring camp in 1984 having played in 57 consecutive games up to the last game of the previous season.<ref name="upiretire">{{cite news|title=The retirement of linebacker Loren Toews leaves just seven...|url=https://upi.com/5318981|access-date=November 1, 2017|work=UPI|date=May 29, 1984}}</ref>

Toews has a wife, Valerie and is also the father of three children: Aaron, Jocelyn and Cassandra. Aaron was a defenseman on the [[Northeastern Huskies men's ice hockey|Northeastern University hockey]] team from 1996 to 1998.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.losaltosonline.com/seasonal-sections/217-sports-archive/16557-J40745 |title=Toews gets a taste of big-time hockey |first=Andy |last=Nystrom |date=December 18, 1996 |work=[[Los Altos Town Crier]] |access-date=November 1, 2017}}</ref> Jocelyn owns an independent record label called [[Lujo Records]].

Toews lives in the San Francisco Bay Area where he and his younger brother [[Jeff Toews|Jeff]] (who also played in the NFL as an offensive lineman) buy and sell real estate.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.apnews.com/3c28d0eb5dff42da93f9908044a883d3 |title=Man's quixotic quest for Super Steelers' autographs ends |last=Gorman |first=Kevin |date=July 11, 2017 |work=[[Associated Press]] |access-date=November 1, 2017}}</ref>

'''Lorenzo LaVonne Neal''' (born December 27, 1970) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[fullback (gridiron football)|fullback]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for 16 seasons. Neal played [[college football]] for the [[Fresno State Bulldogs football|Fresno State Bulldogs]] and was selected by the [[New Orleans Saints]] in the fourth round of the [[1993 NFL draft]]. A four-time [[Pro Bowl]] selection and three-time [[All-Pro]], he was also a member of the [[New York Jets]], the [[Tampa Bay Buccaneers]], the [[Tennessee Titans]], the [[Cincinnati Bengals]], the [[San Diego Chargers]], the [[Baltimore Ravens]] and the [[Oakland Raiders]]. Considered one of the best blocking fullbacks in NFL history,<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.espn.com/blog/nflnation/post/_/id/5946/five-observations-from-oakland-s-minicamp |title=Five observations from Oakland's minicamp |first=Bill |last=Williamson |date=May 11, 2009 |access-date=January 24, 2010 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090804172306/http://myespn.go.com/blogs/nflnation/0-7-770/Five-observations-from-Oakland-s-minicamp.html |archive-date=August 4, 2009}}</ref> Neal blocked for a 1,000-plus-yard running back in 11 straight seasons from 1997 to 2007.{{Citation needed|date=March 2025}}

'''Louis James Kelcher''' (born August 23, 1953)<ref name=pfr/> is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[defensive tackle]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL), spending most of his career with the [[San Diego Chargers]]. He was a four-time [[All-Pro]] and a three-time [[Pro Bowl]] selection. Kelcher was inducted into the [[Los Angeles Chargers Hall of Fame|Chargers Hall of Fame]] and is a member of [[San Diego Chargers 40th Anniversary Team|their 40th]] and [[San Diego Chargers 50th Anniversary Team|50th anniversary team]]s.

Kelcher played [[college football]] with the [[SMU Mustangs football|SMU Mustangs]] and earned consensus [[College Football All-America Team|All-American]] honors as a senior in 1974. He was selected by the Chargers in the second round of the [[1975 NFL draft]]. His outstanding performance made him one of the team's most popular players from 1975 through 1983. He joined the [[San Francisco 49ers]] in 1984 and helped them win [[Super Bowl XIX]] that season.

'''Lewis Vincent Benfatti''' (born March 9, 1971) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player. The 6' 4", 278 lb., [[defensive tackle]] was the third round pick (#94 overall) of the [[New York Jets]] in the [[1994 NFL draft]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=1994 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1994/draft.htm |access-date=2023-03-31 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> He played three seasons (1994–1996) with the Jets. Benfatti was named [[College Football All-America Team|All-American]] and a [[Lombardi Award]] finalist while at [[Penn State University]]. A team captain for the [[Nittany Lions]], he played in the 1994 [[East-West Shrine Game]] and [[Senior Bowl]] games.

He earned a [[Bachelor of Arts]] in [[speech communication]] from Penn State in 1993. Benfatti was an All-State football player and heavyweight [[Wrestling|wrestler]] at [[Morris Knolls High School]] in [[Denville Township, New Jersey]].<ref>Lange, Randy. [http://infoweb.newsbank.com/iw-search/we/InfoWeb?p_action=doc&p_docid=0EAF928F8C4EF40A&p_docnum=1&p_queryname=NaN&p_product=NewsBank&p_theme=aggregated4&p_nbid=I53N59FQMTE4NTg0NzQ0OS4yODY4NjU6MTo3OnJhLTE4ODg "CRUSHING HALT TO JETS CAREER: BROKEN NECK KOS BENFATTI"], ''[[The Record (Bergen County)]]'', April 8, 1997. Accessed August 2, 2007. White played [[college football]] for [[Michigan State Spartans football|Michigan State Spartans]] from 1984 to 1987, and was a consensus [[College Football All-America Team|All-American]] in [[1985 College Football All-America Team|1985]] and [[1987 College Football All-America Team|1987]]. He won the [[Big Ten Most Valuable Player]] in 1987, currently the last Spartan to be selected. He also continues to hold Michigan State records for rushing yardage in a career (4,887), rushing yardage in a season (2,066), rushing touchdowns in a career (43), rushing attempts in a season (419) and rushing attempts in a career (1,082).

White was inducted into the [[College Football Hall of Fame]] in 2019. He has also been inducted into the Michigan State University Hall of Fame (2010), the [[Rose Bowl Hall of Fame]] (2022) and the [[Michigan Sports Hall of Fame]] (2023).

'''Louis James Piccone''' (born July 17, 1949) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[wide receiver]] and [[kick returner]] for nine seasons in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) with the [[New York Jets]] and [[Buffalo Bills]].  He played [[college football]] for the [[West Liberty Hilltoppers football|West Liberty State Hilltoppers]].<ref>{{cite news|url=https://buffalonews.com/sports/bills/erik-brady-looooou-gets-his-due-as-former-bills-player-lou-piccone-is-honored-by/article_a5562a72-3f4d-11ed-840a-0ffa1accf96a.html|title='Looooou!' gets his due as former Bills player Lou Piccone is honored by Jersey home|date=September 28, 2022|agency=[[The Buffalo News]]|author=Brady, Erik|accessdate=September 29, 2022|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20220929102206/https://buffalonews.com/sports/bills/erik-brady-looooou-gets-his-due-as-former-bills-player-lou-piccone-is-honored-by/article_a5562a72-3f4d-11ed-840a-0ffa1accf96a.html|archivedate=September 29, 2022}}</ref>

Raised in [[Vineland, New Jersey]], Piccone played prep football at [[Vineland High School]]; he was honored in 2022 with a street renaming and a key to the city of Vineland, recognizing him as the first athlete from the city to play in the NFL.<ref>McGurk, Tom. [https://www.courierpostonline.com/story/sports/2022/08/30/vinelands-piccone-to-be-honored-by-city-with-street-name-key/65457451007/ "Vineland's first NFL player to be honored by city on Sept. 29 with street name, key"], ''[[The Daily Journal (New Jersey)|The Daily Journal]]'', August 30, 2022. Accessed May 29, 2024. "Lou Piccone, the first Vineland High School football player to compete in the National Football League, will be honored with a street dedication and key to the city on Sept. 29."</ref>

Piccone played with the [[Youngstown Hardhats]] of the [[Midwest Football League (1962–1978)|Midwest Football League]] in 1972.<ref>{{cite news |title=Hardhats' Next Foe Is Flint |url=https://newspapers.com/article/the-plain-dealer/147800298/ |newspaper=The Plain Dealer |via=Newspapers.com |date=August 7, 1972 |access-date=May 21, 2024}}</ref> He played with the [[Bridgeport Jets]] of the [[Atlantic Coast Football League]] in 1973.<ref>{{cite news |author=Weisman, Larry |title=Ex-Jet Piccone is alive and well in Buffalo |url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/99330180/poughkeepsie-journal/ |newspaper=[[Poughkeepsie Journal]] |via=Newspapers.com |date=November 10, 1979 |access-date=May 21, 2024}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |author=Danowski, Jeff |title=Piccone did NFL's dirty work for 9 years |url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/99331057/the-journal-times/ |newspaper=[[The Journal Times]] |via=Newspapers.com |date=July 20, 1995 |access-date=April 8, 2022}}</ref>

Piccone caught 100 passes for 1,380 yards and six touchdowns in nine years in the NFL.

'''Louis Edward Carter''' (February 6, 1953 – October 11, 2020) was an American professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[running back]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played for the [[Oakland Raiders]] and the [[Tampa Bay Buccaneers]]. Born in [[Laurel, Maryland]], he was a third round pick of the Raiders in 1975 having been the MVP of the Coaches' All-American college all-star game in his senior year at Maryland. He came to the Bucs in the veteran allocation draft of 1976 and became a valuable member of the Buc offense during its first three seasons as a running back and occasional receiver out of the backfield. He also threw the first TD pass in franchise history when he was stopped at the line of scrimmage in a game against the Seahawks and then lobbed the ball across the line to receiver Morris Owens for an unlikely one-yard score. He carried the ball 11 times for 27 yards in his rookie season in Oakland and also had two receptions for 29 yards, but never played again in the NFL after leaving Tampa Bay.<ref>{{cite web |title=Louis Carter |url=https://www.bucpower.com/louis-carter.html |website=BucPower.com |accessdate=October 13, 2020}}</ref> After retiring from pro football, Carter sold cars for Covington Buick in [[Silver Spring, Maryland]].<ref>{{cite news |last1=Wagner |first1=Bill |title=Louis Carter, former Maryland football great and Anne Arundel County Sports Hall of Famer, dies |url=https://www.capitalgazette.com/sports/ac-cs-louis-carter-obituary-tribute-20201013-vz5pxjku4ncunpj7aqpjzeuplq-story.html |accessdate=October 13, 2020 |work=[[The Capital]] |date=October 13, 2020}}</ref> When the dealership closed, Carter joined the security team at [[University of Maryland Global Campus]], where he was a security coordinator.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Dempsey |first1=Mary |title=Remembering Louis Carter: A Master at Forging Relationships |url=https://globalmedia.umgc.edu/2020/10/21/remembering-louis-carter-a-master-at-forging-relationships/ |accessdate=October 22, 2020 |website=UMGC Global Media Center |date=October 21, 2020}}</ref>
